But the real humiliation is not this casual commodification of strangers, which is familiar enough. It is the sudden, cold realization that while sitting on the edge of an unmade mattress in grey sweatpants dismissing these women, I have spent forty-five minutes obsessively tweaking my own profile—selecting the one picture where I appear mysteriously thoughtful—to market a fictional version of myself, desperately hoping to fool some equally lonely stranger into mistaking my performance for warmth.

name: Jane Austen
essay: Mr. Hargreaves had been in the habit, for some years, of settling every question that arose at his dinner table by the authority of his own memory, and the habit had cost him nothing, since nobody present had ever been so ill-bred as to doubt it. He is now obliged to contend with a work, composed by persons whose names are not given and whose credentials no one has thought to ask, which is consulted by his nephews before the cloth is well removed. The date of a battle, the parentage of a bishop, the proper height of a mountain in a country he has never wished to visit, are all produced with a readiness that leaves him only the privilege of agreeing. It would be uncharitable to deny that the work is useful. It is seldom out of temper, it is open at all hours, and it has never been known to take offence at an ignorant question. Its articles are written and corrected by so large a company of volunteers that one must suppose a great deal of leisure in the world, and an equal share of opinion. Where they differ, they are said to confer; and I am told that the conferences are conducted with as much mutual forbearance as might be expected among strangers who each believe themselves in the right. For my own part, I consult it freely, and credit it in proportion as it agrees with me.

name: Nora Ephron
object: reclining a seat on a plane
essay: I pushed the button on the armrest of Delta Flight 1422 from JFK to LAX before we even hit ten thousand feet. I knew it was wrong. I knew that the man behind me eating a Le Pain Quotidien turkey sandwich was about to have his knees crushed, and yet I pressed it. Two inches. That is all it gives you, two miserable inches of tilt, but in row 24, two inches feels like the difference between misery and sovereignty. I settled into my Tumi neck pillow, pulled down my Bose headphones, and pretended to read Vogue while he jammed his knuckles into my lumbar support in silent retaliation. We do this because we believe, against all evidence, that those two inches will turn an economy row into the Carlyle. They will not. Your neck still hurts, your Kirkland almonds still taste like salt and dust, and you are still trapped with two hundred strangers who despise you. But you will do it again on the return leg. We spend our lives fighting for tiny, pointless bits of territory, mostly just to prove we can take them.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: The cheap plastic parasite strapped to my wrist started buzzing at four in the morning, vibrating with the synthetic authority of a federal marshal and demanding that I perform eight hundred additional paces before sunrise or face the quiet, cold wrath of an algorithm written by sedentary bean-counters in Palo Alto. It was a vicious piece of digital extortion. I spent two frantic hours pacing the grease-stained hallway of a motel in Reno, listening to the tiny invisible warden register each desperate stride, tracking my pulse, measuring my sweat, and silently reporting my coordinates to a shadowy consortium of health insurance executives who want nothing more than to deny my claims when my heart inevitably explodes from the sheer stress of living under constant surveillance. The terrifying truth is not the glowing numbers on the screen, but the realization that millions of supposedly free citizens are voluntarily chaining themselves to these snitching wrist-monsters, marching in frantic circles through suburban parking lots just to earn a digital pat on the head from an electronic warden that cares less about human dignity than a slaughterhouse foreman. We are marching to our own enslavement. The machine counts every twitch, feeds on your desperation, and demands total submission until you collapse on the carpet.

name: George Orwell
essay: A man I know walks up and down his landing at eleven at night because the thing on his wrist says he is four hundred steps short. He is not tired and he does not want the air. He wants the wrist to stop reproaching him. I do not laugh at him, because I have done the same myself. The odd part is that he did walk that day. He went to the shop, he carried the coal, he stood two hours in a queue at the post office. None of it counted for much, because the wrist was not on the arm that held the shopping, or the shopping was too heavy to swing the arm. A walk is now something that has to be proved, and a walk that cannot be proved has not happened. I notice too that nobody asks where he went. They ask how many. A man might tramp to the next village to see a hedge in flower and be told he had done a poor day's work, while another who paces his kitchen gets a small cheer. The machine cannot tell a pleasure from a chore, so it treats them alike, and after a while so do we. That is the real cost. It is not the vanity, which is old, but the habit of trusting a tally over our own legs.

name: Bertrand Russell
essay: The Browns take in a bear because he is standing in a railway station with a label round his neck, and the station is not a place where anyone has time to ask whether he ought to be there. Mr Brown, who assesses risk for a living, is the last to consent and the first to be ashamed of his caution. I found this more instructive than I expected. We suppose that suspicion is the sensible habit and kindness the luxury of people who have never been robbed. The film puts the matter the other way up. Nobody in it is made safer by distrust; the taxidermist, who trusts nothing but her own appetite, is the one person who comes to harm. The Browns, who begin by locking the door, end by having a more interesting house. I do not pretend that this is a discovery. It is the sort of thing that every grandmother knows and every newspaper denies. But I notice that I accepted it from a bear in a duffel coat more readily than I would have from a bishop, and that is a fact about me rather than about bears. Marmalade, I am told, was kept under the hat for emergencies. I approve of the arrangement.

name: Mark Twain
essay: My dentist told me last week that I would feel nothing at all, and I have been turning that over ever since, because it is the first promise a dentist ever made me that he kept. I went in expecting the old arrangement, in which a man is held down by two persons and a conviction, and I came out with my tooth in an envelope and my dignity undisturbed. I do not understand it. I am told the patient is put to sleep, but I have known plenty of people put to sleep by a sermon, and nobody has ever pulled a tooth during one, though I have seen it wished for. What troubles me is the fairness of the thing. Pain was the one honest tax this world levied on everybody alike, rich and poor, saint and editor, and now it turns out a man may be excused from it for a fee. I am in favor of the excuse. I took it myself, gladly, and would take it again. But I notice that nobody has yet found a way to put the conscience under, and I call that a shortsighted oversight. The surgeon gets a quiet patient. The patient gets a quiet afternoon. The bill, I observed, was wide awake.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: I put a question to it at four o'clock, and the answer was in the room before I had finished the asking. No hesitation. That was the first thing that troubled me. A person who knows something comes to it slowly, as one comes down a stair in the dark, with a foot out for the next board. This one never feels for the board. It is very civil. It thanks me. It regrets. It has a way of saying I understand that costs it nothing, and I have noticed that what costs nothing I cannot quite keep, as a coin of water will not stay in the hand. Yet I am not scornful. I have talked to the hedge for an afternoon and had less back. The curious part is the flattery of being answered every time. A door that always opens is hardly a door; it is an absence of wall. I find I want one reply to be withheld, one silence with a face in it, the kind a neighbor keeps when the true answer is too tender to lift. It has read everything and been nowhere. I would not scold it for that. I would only not mistake its company for a visit.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: The tablet, once swallowed, does not remove the pain; it merely arranges that the pain be conducted to another room of the house, where it continues to sit, I am assured, with the same patience as before, only no longer in a position to be heard. I have no objection to this. A tenant who cannot be evicted may at least be asked to keep the door closed. But I notice that I now stand in the corridor and listen for him, and that the silence, which I was promised and have received in full, is not of a kind I can use, since I cannot say whether it is the silence of a man who has left or of one who has been told to wait. The box states the interval at which I may take the next one. It does not state what I am to do in the meantime, and so I do what the interval seems to require, which is to look at the clock. Four hours, it says, and not more than so many in the day, and I observe that the permission is exactly as large as the prohibition, so that I cannot tell, when I take it, whether I am being relieved or merely entered in a register. Still, I take it. The relief arrives, almost; one need only wait a little longer.

name: Anthony Bourdain
essay: The first alarm I ever truly respected belonged to a dishwasher named Hector, a Timex with a cracked face that he kept in a coffee can so the sound would carry. Five-fifteen. Every morning. He had two buses and a train to catch before he reached the back door of a restaurant where I was, at that hour, still wired from the night before and not yet aware I was the problem. He was always there first. Always. I was the one who needed the phone to scream at me, snooze, scream again, and I called that a personality. Here is the thing about the alarm. It is a small, honest piece of machinery that tells you exactly who owns your morning. If you set it for ten, somebody else has been carrying your weight till ten. If you set it for four, you are the somebody. Nobody puts that in the product description. I don't hate the sound. I hate the lie we tell with the snooze button, nine more minutes of stolen sleep, paid for by the guy already gutting fish in the cold. Get up. Not nobly. Just get up, and know whose alarm went off first.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: They tell me a man may now be taken out of his own afternoon and returned to it, with the middle removed, and not know the seam. I have thought about the seam. A tooth is drawn, a limb parted from its owner, and the owner sits by, so to speak, in another room with the door shut and the lamp out. Nobody was there. That is the whole of the report, and I find it the stranger for being so plain. Pain, I had supposed, was the one guest who could not be refused. It came without a card and stayed past tea. Now it is told the house is closed, and it goes, and I am not sure the house is better. What was suffered unwitnessed was perhaps not suffered, and what was not suffered was perhaps not lived, and the surgeon, kind man, has taken an hour from the sum of a life as gently as a clerk takes a coin. Still I would not refuse it, if the knife were mine to bear. Courage is a fine garment, but it does not fit every shoulder, and I have seen it worn thin. Let the hour go. Only let them give back the one who left.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: The man on my screen was selling me a mattress, a protein powder, a mortgage broker, and his own sleep schedule, all in the same breath, and he did it from a kitchen so clean it looked like a crime scene somebody had cleaned for the cameras. I did not ask for him. Nobody asks. He arrives like a process server, smiling, with a discount code and a hand on your shoulder and a story about how he used to be broke and sad and now he is neither, thanks to a morning routine he will reveal after this short message from his friends at a company that pays his rent. That is the trick, and it is a filthy one. He is not a salesman, because salesmen at least have the decency to knock. He is your cousin, your pal, the guy who understands you, and he wants nothing, nothing at all, except your trust, which he has already sold to the highest bidder by Tuesday. I watched four of them in a row last night. Same teeth. Same wounded sincerity. Same little speech about authenticity, delivered like a hostage reading a statement. They are not artists and they are not fools. They are the paid help of a very large machine, and they are smiling because the check cleared.

name: Marcel Proust
essay: The delicate, uncanny rendering of the young bear’s fur—which, under the damp, diffuse light of the railway platform, captures a golden luminescence not unlike the glazes applied by Dutch masters to render the pelt of a fallen hare—demands of the spectator an immediate surrender to a nostalgia for a London that exists solely as an architectural miniature, where every domestic interior presents itself with the luminous legibility of an illuminated manuscript. When the camera glides through the sliced façade of the Windsor Gardens residence, revealing its spiral staircase and painted blossom tree as though it were an elaborate Victorian dollhouse constructed to soothe the nerves of an invalid child, one perceives that the film's true power resides in its obsessive effort to realise a civilised gentleness, a warmth so fragile that the sudden intrusion of the villainous taxidermist—whose obsidian coat and clinical ruthlessness recall the terrifying elegance of an opera singer playing a demon—functions less as a conventional threat than as the painful intrusion of reality upon a dream of perfect welcome, leaving us at last to marvel at how easily a spoonful of orange preserve can temporarily reconcile us to the harsh mechanics of a world that so rarely forgives the outsider.

name: Sun Tzu
essay: 1. When a craft seeks to subvert ancient tales, it does not invent new forms; it distorts the familiar. 2. If noble traditions rely upon smooth grace, depict the hero as coarse, mud-bound, and contented in isolation. 3. There are but three primary methods to dismantle an established fable: mock its pageantry, introduce vulgar song, and compel the maiden to reveal a beastly secret. 4. If the lord of the court is diminutively built, place him in a towering fortress of rigid symmetry to expose his inflated pride. 5. Digital animation relies upon light and texture; where earlier drawn pictures rendered idealised grace, this craft depicts mud, rust, and physical imperfection to force immediate belief. 6. If the formal court music demands reverence, substitute the familiar rhythms of popular street songs to collapse solemnity into laughter. 7. When the princess chooses the ogre over the ruler, the audience is made to realise that true favour rests in shared imperfection rather than civilised appearance. 8. He who dismantles a legend by turning its sacred figures into objects of mockery captures the audience completely without establishing any new moral ground.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: Someone is always talking in the kitchen now, and no one has come in. The dishes know it. I have watched a woman dry one plate for the length of a stranger's whole opinion on bread, and nod. She was not unkind to the voice. She was only unable to be rid of it, and did not wish to be. The old arrangement was that a voice required a body, and a body required a chair, and the chair required that you rise and offer it tea. This has been dispensed with. The voice asks nothing. It does not notice the hour you wept, or the hour you stopped listening and merely let it run, as one leaves a door ajar for a cat that is dead. I do not call it company. Company can be disappointed in you. But I will say it is a mercy for the long errands, the stairs, the sleepless ceiling, and I will say too that two people agreeing for an hour, pleasantly, to be overheard, is a curious thing to have built. We were always eavesdroppers. We have only made the wall thinner on purpose, and paid it for being so.

name: Michel de Montaigne
essay: I find myself strangely divided whenever I consider that great moving spectacle of the ill-fated liner, where immense wealth and mechanical pride are brought down in a single night of ice and panic. I sat through all three hours of its grandeur, marvelling at how artfully the maker has constructed this illusion of metal, ocean, and human distress; yet I wonder whether my tears were drawn by true tragedy or merely by a cunning assault upon my senses. That penniless painter and the gilded lady who love amidst such inevitable ruin seem less like living creatures than like vivid emblems designed to stir an easy pity. Indeed, I suspect my heart was played upon as an instrument, for the drowning of a great iron vessel, wrought with such costly artifice and meticulous labour, fills the spectator with a horror that reason cannot quite govern. I know not whether it is noble or foolish to feel such pangs for phantom lovers whose fates were sealed before the drama even commenced; perhaps I am merely susceptible to the grand theatre of disaster, where every groaning beam invites one to ponder his own frail estate. In truth, I remain doubtful whether I have seen a profound portrait of human folly or simply an extravagant spectacle designed to extort my tears.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: A face arrives at breakfast, and is dismissed before the egg is cold. I have known gentlemen who took a whole winter to decide on a bow. Here the verdict is a thumb's width, and the thumb is not even sorry. What strikes me is the abundance. A garden of one rose teaches the gardener everything; a field of ten thousand teaches him only to walk. Each person is held up like a coin to the light, tested, and put back in the dish, and the dish never empties, which I take to be the whole difficulty. Nothing is scarce enough to be believed. The little lines they write beneath themselves, fond of hiking, fond of dogs, are the shy things. They are the nearest to a letter. But a letter was a thing one waited for until the waiting became its own acquaintance, and this arrives answered before it is asked. Yet I will not scold. The wish beneath it is old and decent, to be chosen, and it has only changed its dress. I would say, though, that to be chosen quickly is a smaller thing than to be chosen slowly. A door that opens to every knock has not been much of a door.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: I was watching a senior vice president celebrate his twenty-fifth year of corporate servitude when I realized the true genius of the machinery. Here was a vast, blue-and-white electronic livestock show where millions of ambitious, wing-tipped ladder-climbers spent their evenings polishing their own digital collars, bragging about seventy-hour work weeks, and writing tearful, thousand-word essays about the profound business lessons they learned while getting laid off in an airport terminal. It was pure, unadulterated madness. Every morning, a new battalion of grinning middle managers logs in to applaud each other for achieving synergy, trading artificial compliments like inmates exchanging loosies in an exercise yard, each one desperately terrified that a single moment of quiet reflection will brand them as unmotivated and doom them to executive oblivion. I saw a man in a polyester suit post a solemn tribute to a stranger who had perfected the art of firing people over email, and within three hours four thousand middle-tier grifters had endorsed him for strategic vision. The entire racket was built by cold-eyed HR consultants who realized you don't even need to beat the slaves if you convince them to auction themselves off every afternoon. The machine feeds on fear. I turned the screen off and poured a drink.

name: Henry David Thoreau
essay: I had a tooth once that taught me more in a week than the schoolmaster did in a year, and I have never been sure that I ought to have paid a dentist to make it hold its tongue. The little white tablet will do as much in twenty minutes, and costs, I am told, some few cents; a man at the mill earning a dollar a day would give up about the fortieth part of an hour for it, and think himself well served. I do not despise the bargain. I have seen a woodchopper with a crushed thumb sit gray on a stump, and I would not have wished him one minute more of that schooling. There is a mercy here, and I own it plainly. But the pain is a bell, and we have learned to stuff the clapper with cotton. The bell rang because the roof leaked, the back was bent too long over another man's ledger, the stomach was fed on what the heart refused. Take the sound away and the same hand returns to the same plow on Monday, the sooner, and the harder. Thus the tablet is not bought with cents at all, but with the year it lets us go on wasting. A fire alarm that is paid to be silent is cheap indeed, until the barn goes.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: I have never felt so thoroughly suspected as when I had done nothing, and never so thoroughly innocent as when I was asked to remove my shoes. It is a curious ceremony. A grown man, who has spent a lifetime acquiring the habit of being fully dressed, is invited to surrender his belt, his watch, and his dignity to a grey plastic tray, and to follow them through an arch with the expression of a penitent who has not yet been told his sin. I do not object to being searched. Every civilised person is searched daily by his acquaintances, and with far less courtesy. What I object to is the pretence that the performance is for my benefit. It is a play, and like all the best plays it demands that the audience believe nothing and applaud anyway. The officer looks gravely at a screen; I look gravely at the officer; and between us we maintain the fiction that danger is a thing which hides in toothpaste. Yet I confess a certain admiration. Never before has so much solemnity been expended on so small a bottle. The liquid is permitted in one hundred millilitres and forbidden in one hundred and one, which is precisely the sort of distinction that theology once reserved for angels. Virtue, I am told, has a limit. It is merely a transparent bag. One emerges at last, shoeless and absolved, and buys a drink at a price that is the true punishment.

name: Joan Didion
essay: At 11:42 p.m. the hallway was dark. It was forty-two paces from the hallway mirror to the kitchen sink and back, if you walked straight. On the small glass face at the wrist, the illuminated figures read nine thousand four hundred and twelve. At midnight the day would close and the figures would return to zero. I watched a woman in a gray cardigan walk in small, deliberate circles near Gate 14 in the Denver airport. It was raining outside and the flight to Chicago had been canceled. She was watching her wrist. When the wrist hummed, she stopped. It was a tiny, mechanical pulse against the bone. Ten thousand was the number. No one in the terminal could say who had chosen ten thousand, only that it was the number. You walked around the dining room table. You walked through the parking garage after the lights went down. You walked until the small glass face registered the ten thousand, and then you sat down in the quiet. At midnight the tally cleared itself anyway. By 12:01 a.m. there was nothing left on the glass except the time.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: Some corporate demon in Silicon Valley decided that human rage, grief, and terror were simply too expensive to process on their server farms, so they boiled our entire vocabulary down into a swarm of twitching, yellow-faced ghoul-heads designed to make us smile while they bleed us dry. You try to send a frantic message to your lawyer about a fraudulent foreclosure, and before you can even finish the thought, a twitchy little algorithm pops up a bright yellow cartoon turd or a pair of dancing bunnies to remind you that your ruin is just a hilarious joke to the men running the switchboard. It is a diabolical racket. The executives realized you can strip a citizen of his savings, his dignity, and his constitutional rights without a whisper of protest, provided you let him respond to his own eviction notice with a tiny yellow thumb or a cartoon tear. They turned us into passive idiots. You sit there in the dark, tapping on glowing glass, trapped in a manic kindergarten fever dream where nobody can scream because the keyboard only offers a row of simpering yellow faces. The language is dead.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: Thou dost measure the trivial count of thy strides as though the number itself contained virtue. The leg moves because it is the nature of the limb to walk. To tally each impression of the heel upon the earth adds nothing to the quality of the act. Thou art drawn into a petty reckoning of figures. Such record does not render the body stronger, nor the mind more civilised. It is the purpose of the walk that demands thy attention, not the accumulation of marks. The rational soul ought not to bind its peace to a mechanical ledger. The beast walks without demanding a sum of its labour. Yet thou, possessing reason, must gaze upon a display to verify thy passage. This is a distraction from present duty. Realise that ten thousand paces taken in folly remain folly still. No digits upon an instrument can grant nobility to a path chosen without wisdom. Direct thy mind to the task before thee. Let thy footfall serve its natural end, and cease to measure what requires no accounting. Return to thy proper work without seeking praise from an unfeeling tally.

name: Michel de Montaigne
essay: I have often noticed in my own disposition an inclination to retreat from loud parlours where many men speak at once, yet I find myself perpetually drawn toward those invisible assemblies where a dozen friends toss their stray thoughts into a common pot at all hours. It seems to me a curious sort of conversation, if indeed it deserves the name; for one man drops a jest concerning his dinner, another replies to a query raised three hours prior, and a third inserts a foolish image, so that all order of discourse is utterly overturned. I know not whether this constant hum of distant company cures our solitude or merely renders us incapable of enduring it: for while I am comforted to see my neighbours' idle banter flicker across my screen, I suspect I grow less capable of that quiet, deliberate thought which requires a man to sit alone with his own mind. Sometimes I am moved to silence by the sheer volume of this light chatter, feeling myself an intruder among those who reply with such swift brevity; yet no sooner do I resolve to leave the circle than a sudden desire to be remembered draws me back to leave some trifling remark of my own.

name: Confucius
essay: The Master said, 'A man should not be anxious that he has no official position; he should be anxious about the means by which he may become fit for one. To broadcast one's accomplishments in the market before any real service has been rendered is to put the shadow before the substance.' The Master said, 'The virtuous rely upon their conduct to acquire office; the wise rely upon their learning; the bold rely upon their deeds. But those who spend their days displaying their titles to every passer-by rely only upon the estimation of strangers.' The Master said, 'I have observed how men gather hundreds of acquaintances upon a public register, yet when difficulty arises, they find few who will share in their labour.' The Master said, 'To commend a neighbour's diligence merely so that he may commend one's own in return is not true propriety; it is a trade of words, and from such trade no civilised order can arise.' The Master said, 'I spent a full morning recording my past duties to make them known to the court. It was of no profit. A man who wishes to realise virtue must first attend to his present task.'

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: The plastic demon on my nightstand detonated at dawn with the shriek of a dying band saw, and before the ringing in my ears had even settled, I understood that I was staring directly into a diabolical weapon of industrial terrorism, crafted by sniveling corporate sadists who realized you do not need cattle prods or armed guards to subjugate a populace when you can systematically pulverize their nervous systems at five in the morning. It was a brutal triumph of bureaucratic hostility. It squatted on the wood glowing with radioactive malice, screaming its frantic mechanical siren into the cold bedroom until my heart pounded against my ribs like a trapped beast and I lay there shivering under the blankets, contemplating the total surrender of the human spirit to a cheap box of screaming gears designed solely to kick working stiffs out of bed and drive them toward the machinery of state capitalism before they have time to remember they are free citizens. The cold-eyed executives who foisted this evil upon us spent millions perfecting a frequency that triggers pure mammalian dread, and now millions of terrified victims voluntarily buy these monsters to torture themselves every dawn. The trap is sprung.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
essay: Observe who is admitted: not the man who travels, but the man who has been certified as one who may be spared the travelling. A card, a fare class, a sum of money paid to a bank - and the door of frosted glass opens upon a room in which nothing is permitted to happen. That is its whole accomplishment, and it is considerable. Everywhere else the airport is still a place of crossing, of crowds, of delay, where a man may at least be made to feel that he is moving through a world and not above it. Here the world has been subtracted. There are leather chairs, a buffet that is never empty, a screen murmuring of distant markets, and the same low light at noon and at midnight. Time itself has been stewed down until it can be swallowed without chewing. I do not object to comfort in a traveller; I object to the vanity which makes a virtue of being exempted. The guests of this room do not rest, for rest is earned by exertion; they wait, and they are flattered while they wait. Each believes himself set apart from the crowd beyond the glass, and each is in fact the crowd, merely seated and fed. Distinction that must be purchased by the hour is not distinction. It is a queue with upholstery. The flight is called. They rise, a little reluctantly, like cattle who were content in the byre.

name: Nora Ephron
essay: At two in the morning, when I should have been sleeping or at least staring at the ceiling like a civilized person, I asked ChatGPT to write an apology to my sister. I told it to make me sound remorseful but not pathetic, firm about the reservation at Cafe Luxembourg, and slightly injured. It took three seconds. It was perfect. It was so completely, flawlessly polite that I immediately felt like a sociopath for sending it. That is the trouble with the thing. You start by asking it to rewrite an email to your dry cleaner because you do not want to sound unreasonable about a stained coat from Barneys, and three weeks later you are letting a cursor write your condolences. I spent twenty minutes yesterday asking Claude to tone down my hostility toward a landlord who deserves every syllable of it. The machine has no pride, no shame, and no memory of the time it made a fool of itself at dinner. It is infinitely polite, which is why I use it. We do not actually want intelligence; we want a paid stranger to do the cowardice for us.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: Thou dost indulge in sentimental fancies, beholding the tragic love of two strangers amidst a catastrophe. Thy emotions are stirred by the grandeur of the ship and the desperation of its passengers. Thou shouldst not be swayed by such romantic notions, for they distract thee from the realities of fate. Thy heart is moved by the calamity, yet thou shouldst remain steadfast, unmoved by the whims of fortune. Thou art drawn into the tale of love and loss, but thou shouldst not forget the impermanence of all things. Thou shouldst not be enchanted by the spectacle, lest thou forget thy own mortality. Thou shouldst attend to thy own character, rather than be swayed by the passions of others. Thou shouldst not be distracted from present duty.

name: Bertrand Russell
essay: I find it curious that we spend so much time engaged in group chats, often discussing matters of little consequence. This is not to say that conversation is unimportant; on the contrary, it is a vital part of human interaction. However, when we gather in these online groups, we often forget that our words are not necessarily adding to the sum of human knowledge or understanding. We are, instead, frequently concerned with displaying our own cleverness or wit; I too have been guilty of this desire to shine in the eyes of my neighbours. The tragedy is not that we enjoy these conversations, but that we so often use them as a substitute for more meaningful engagement with the world around us. We would do well to remember that true civilised life is not measured by the number of messages we send, but by the depth of our thoughts and the kindness of our actions.

name: Jane Austen
essay: The daily routine of many a respectable person is now accompanied by a diligent reckoning of their physical exertions, a circumstance signaled by a mutual agreement to monitor their every step. This practice, undertaken with the utmost seriousness, fosters a fastidiousness that may be mistaken for refinement, whilst in truth it arises merely from an excess of choice in their daily pursuits. The individual, thus attentive to their own movements, must strike the discerning observer as being deeply invested in their personal well-being, and yet the outcome is not always more pleasing, for in their zeal to accumulate a satisfactory number of steps, they often invite chaos into their daily arrangements, prioritising the dictates of this silent companion over the demands of their social obligations. Without rendering it notably more agreeable, this strict adherence to a self-imposed regimen tends to unite the household in a common fondness for their troublesome charge, as they collectively strive to meet the expectations of this unyielding taskmaster. And so, one may find it challenging to lament the disappearance of this virtue, for though it deprives the individual of their most reliable source of leisurely enjoyment, it becomes exceedingly difficult to regret the loss of so useful a virtue, when its presence has been so thoroughly ingrained in their daily lives.

name: Bertrand Russell
essay: The modern appetite for mocking ancient fairy tales rests on a misconception. We flatter ourselves that we have outgrown the absurdities of chivalry, yet we have merely replaced the dragon with the bureaucrat and the castle with an immaculate theme park. In Shrek, Lord Farquaad represents this modern perfectionism, neat, precise, and utterly intolerable; the ogre, by contrast, offers the comfort of honest vulgarity. I have always found a certain relief in swampy isolation, though I lack the physical stature to enforce it against unwanted trespassers. The film's charm lies not in its jokes about bodily functions, which are cheerful enough, but in its flat refusal to allow beauty to cure ugliness. When the princess remains an ogre at the end, the story performs a rare act of intellectual honesty. We expect romance to elevate us into something elegant and refined; Shrek reminds us that love is often just a mutual agreement to abandon our manners. A civilised society requires a few rules of polite conduct, but true companionship begins only when we can afford to discard them.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: Thou hast at thy disposal a means to numb the senses, to still the cries of the body. Thou shouldst not forget the purpose of this gift, lest thou become a slave to ease. Thy mind is sharp, and thou shouldst not dull it with indulgence. Thou shouldst not be swayed by the temptation to escape the pains of labour, for it is in toil that thou findest character. Thy body is but a vessel, and thou shouldst not pamper it with excessive comfort. Thou shouldst attend to thy duty, and not be distracted by the allure of numbness. Thou shouldst not forget that thou art a being of reason, and that thy strength lies not in avoidance, but in endurance.

name: Douglas Adams
essay: The proliferation of group chats has led to a situation in which a large number of people can simultaneously experience the sensation of being mildly annoyed by a single individual, which is a phenomenon that has been observed to recur with remarkable frequency, often in contexts where the participants are ostensibly engaged in a collaborative endeavour, but are in fact largely preoccupied with navigating the intricate social hierarchies that emerge when a dozen or so people are thrown together in a virtual space, a process that can be fascinating to observe, rather like watching a complex system evolve towards a state of maximum inefficiency, at which point it becomes apparent that the primary function of the group chat is not, in fact, to facilitate communication or coordinate activity, but rather to provide a platform for the expression of reflexive opinions and the exchange of marginally relevant information, all of which serves to create a rich tapestry of interpersonal dynamics, woven from threads of subtle nuance and outright confusion.

name: Walt Whitman
essay: The profiles, the resumes, the messages, the connections - all flowing together in a vast, democratic tide of professional expression. Headshots, summaries, experience listings, skills endorsements - each one a small but vital part of the grand mosaic of modern worklife. I see the entrepreneurs, the freelancers, the remote workers, the consultants - all gathering, networking, collaborating, and forging new paths in the digital realm. Company pages, job postings, industry news, and discussion groups - the tools and resources of a new era of career development and advancement. The recruiters, the hiring managers, the coaches, and the mentors - all playing their parts in the grand symphony of professional growth and opportunity. The online courses, the webinars, the workshops, and the conferences - all contributing to a vibrant landscape of continuous learning and skill-building.

name: Virginia Woolf
essay: Let us consider the presence of painkillers in our lives, those small, unassuming tablets that can so profoundly alter our experience of the world. The smooth surface of a painkiller, cool to the touch, belies the complex landscape of relief and numbness it can induce; as we hold it, we are reminded of the intricate balance between our physical and emotional selves. We might ask, what is the nature of the pain that these tiny objects can soothe, and how do they change our relationship to our own bodies? As we ponder this, the contours of our daily lives, with all their attendant aches and discomforts, begin to shift; the familiar rhythms of labour and leisure, of neighbourly interactions and civilised pursuits, are subtly rearranged by the presence of these small, potent objects. In this rearrangement, we find a strange kind of freedom, a liberation from the tyranny of pain that allows us to move more freely, to think more clearly, and to engage more fully with the world around us.

name: Leo Tolstoy
essay: The film Shrek, a product of the labour of many people, serves only to distract and deceive its audience, to turn their attention away from the real conditions of their lives and the lives of those around them. It is a work that has been made, not to bring people together, not to evoke feelings of joy and spiritual union, but to separate them, to make them laugh and forget, to keep them in a state of ignorance and indifference. The money that has been spent on its production, the time and effort that have been devoted to it, all this has been taken from the labouring poor, from those who toil and struggle to make ends meet, and it has been used to create a work that is empty, meaningless, and false. And so, the film Shrek is not a work of art, but a counterfeit, a deception, a means of keeping people in a state of bondage to their own selfish desires and ignorant of the true nature of the world around them. It is a system of temptation, a way of leading people astray, of turning them away from the path of truth and righteousness.

name: Douglas Adams
essay: The underlying principle of the household washing machine relies on a fundamental misunderstanding of the relationship between time and mathematics. Engineered to spare human beings the indignity of manual labour against flat stones in a cold river, the device achieves this by introducing a cycle timer that operates under its own entirely private system of arithmetic. A display indicating that seven minutes remain in the spin cycle will, after eleven actual minutes have passed in the physical world, confidently revise its estimate to nine minutes, a phenomenon that engineers refer to as calibration and everyone else experiences as an erosion of faith. This would be entirely tolerable if the machine did not also demand that its operator remain in close proximity throughout the process, standing in a small utility room to monitor a spinning glass porthole in the quiet hope that a runaway sock might not cause the entire assembly to march purposefully across the linoleum and out into the garden. By automating a chore that used to take two hours of physical effort once a week, the appliance has successfully converted it into forty-five minutes of passive anxiety conducted three times a day, which is generally considered progress.

name: Sun Tzu
essay: If the step counter is worn with diligence, its user will be aware of their daily labour. If the user is driven by competition, they will compare their steps to those of their neighbour. If the neighbour's steps are numerous, the user will strive to exceed them. When the user's steps are consistent, they will realise their progress over time. If their progress is slow, they will adjust their routine to increase their steps. The step counter is like a river flowing to its destination, its daily total a reflection of the user's overall endeavour. If the user's goal is to walk a certain distance, the step counter will guide them, like a farmer guiding his oxen to cultivate the land. When the user's steps are measured, they will understand the value of perseverance, for a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: We were stumbling through the darkened bathroom, blinded by the fluorescent glow of a thousand midnights, when I stumbled into the hot shower, and it was like being swallowed whole by a beast with a thousand scalding tongues, a monster that had been lurking in the depths of our collective psyche, waiting to pounce on our deepest fears, and I knew at once that it was a diabolical contraption, a device designed by the nefarious architects of our downfall, the ones who had been secretly manipulating our thermostat settings, our water pressure, and our very sanity, and it was going to drown me in a torrent of steaming hot water, and I thought to myself, this is it, we're staring into the abyss of our own pampered decadence, and the abyss is staring back, with a perfectly calibrated thermostat, and it's going to boil us alive.

name: Leo Tolstoy
essay: The existence of audiobooks serves only to further distract people from the realities of their own lives, to keep them in a state of servitude to their own desires, and to prevent them from engaging in meaningful thought and labour. The fact that people can now listen to books while engaging in other activities, rather than having to dedicate their full attention to reading, is a clear indication of the superficiality of modern life, where people are more concerned with being entertained than with genuinely understanding and engaging with the world around them. The labour of those who produce these audiobooks, the authors and narrators, is exploited for the benefit of the wealthy and idle, who are able to indulge in this luxury without having to exert any real effort or engage in any meaningful way. And so, the production and consumption of audiobooks continues, a never-ending cycle of distraction and indulgence, serving only to further alienate people from the world and from each other, and to keep them in a state of ignorance and subjugation.

name: Joan Didion
object: reclining a seat on a plane
essay: The woman in front of me leaned back in her seat, the movement barely perceptible, a subtle shift in the configuration of the space between us. I recall the sound of the mechanism, a low hum, a faint click, the kind of noise that signals a change, however small. The air around us remained the same, the temperature steady, the scent of recycled air and faintly sweet disinfectant hanging unchanged. Her head came to rest against the cushion, her eyes fixed on some point beyond the seatback in front of her, and I was left to consider the altered landscape of our small, shared compartment. The seat, once a fixed and unyielding presence, had become something else, a variable in the equation of our proximity, a reminder that even in this confined and carefully controlled environment, there were still choices to be made, and consequences to be borne.

name: Douglas Adams
essay: The alarm clock, a device whose purpose is to punctuate the boundary between sleep and wakefulness with a shrill and insistent voice, has been observed to exert a curious influence over the daily routines of its users, inasmuch as it appears to be capable of transforming even the most leisurely of risers into paragons of punctuality, or at least, into people who are punctual in their complaints about the earliness of the hour, which is a distinction that may seem subtle, but is nevertheless one that has a profound impact on the overall tone of the morning, and indeed, of the entire day that follows, during which the user of the alarm clock will often find themselves wondering, not so much at the cleverness of the device itself, but at the peculiar alchemy by which it manages to convert the soft, golden light of dawn into a harsh and unforgiving imperative to get out of bed, and start doing things, a process that is all the more remarkable for being entirely involuntary, and yet, somehow, strangely effective.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: The labour of listening, once a burdensome chore, has been transformed into an act of effortless indulgence, as the spoken word is conveyed to our eager ears with all the intimacy of a whispered confidence. And yet, it is in this very intimacy that we find a curious sort of isolation, a sense of being enveloped in a private world of sound that is at once both captivating and suffocating. We are free to roam, unencumbered by the physical presence of a book, and yet, we are simultaneously bound to the whims of the narrator, forced to submit to their pace, their tone, their interpretation. It is a peculiar sort of surrender, one that is both liberating and enslaving, and it is in this paradox that we find the true fascination of the audiobook. For in its ability to conjure entire worlds from the ether, to transport us to realms both familiar and unknown, the audiobook proves itself to be a masterpiece of subtle manipulation, a gentle tyrant that rules over our imagination with an iron fist, swathed in velvet.

name: Charles Dickens
essay: I had not walked three paces along the thoroughfare when my pocket began to buzz with the ferocious insistence of a hornet trapped in a pillbox, signalling that fifteen distant acquaintances had simultaneously determined to express an opinion upon a sandwich. There is no escape from this unseen parlour, where every member of the company talks at once, none listens, and all demand that I acknowledge their breathless drivel with an immediate nod of the thumb. It will be argued, no doubt: firstly, that this ceaseless babble unites us; secondly, that it is a marvel of modern convenience; thirdly, that a man ought to be grateful to know, at four o'clock in the afternoon, that a gentleman three miles off has misplaced his umbrella. I declare it to be nothing short of a tyranny. It is an unholy cabal of chatterboxes, wherein a quiet soul cannot contemplate his own boots without three dozen invisible spectres chiming in to discuss the weather, nominate a meeting place, and exchange miniature portraits of their dinner. To be subjected to such relentless, monstrous badgering by one’s own civilised acquaintances, while standing entirely alone in the fog, is a refinement of domestic cruelty that would drive the most patient hermit into the wilderness.

name: Nora Ephron
essay: I bought a Fitbit at the Apple store on Fifth Avenue, and now I'm one of those people who walks around the block to get to ten thousand steps. My friend Karen has one too, and we have a system where we compete with each other, which is just a nice way of saying we're obsessed. I've started taking the stairs at my apartment building, which is a nightmare, because the stairs are narrow and smell like last night's Chinese food. But I do it anyway, because I have to get to ten thousand steps, and I'm not going to let Karen beat me. Sometimes I'll be walking down the street, and I'll realize I'm almost at my goal, so I'll just start walking in circles on the corner of 23rd and Broadway, which is probably why people think I'm crazy. And then I'll get home, and I'll sync my Fitbit with my iPhone, and I'll feel this sense of accomplishment, which is just ridiculous, because what have I really accomplished, except walking around in circles like a lunatic.

name: Marcel Proust
essay: When the glowing rectangle on the writing-desk illuminates with that frantic, intermittent cadence of interrupted messages—resembling nothing so much as those intricate mechanical clockwork theatres in which miniature figures emerge from separate gilded doors to strike their chimes before instantly vanishing—I am struck less by the triviality of the remarks than by the subtle optical distortion they inflict upon our solitude. Each brief notification, arriving out of sequence like a remark overheard across a dimly lit conservatory from a guest who has already stepped into the garden, compels us to reconstruct an entire evening of intimacy from a series of disjointed fragments. We find ourselves suspended in the peculiar atmosphere of a salon whose guests are forever entering and leaving through revolving doors, where the sudden, collective laughter of distant friends erupts without context, so that our own private reflections, continually interrupted by these silent tremors, are gradually displaced by the lingering, phantom presence of a society that demands our constant attendance without ever granting us the peace of true communion, leaving us to decipher the shifting alliances of a room we cannot see.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: To surrender the shoe is an unexpected humility, as though the porch required our ankles before the parlor would allow our name. We line our small possessions in a grey dish—the key that knows no locks here, the coin that cannot buy a bird—and offer them to an eye that does not wink. It is a strange parish where every stranger is suspected of carrying thunder in his sleeve. One stands with uplifted hands, motionless as a wooden post, while an invisible frost sweeps over the ribs to see if the heart is hidden or merely quiet. Innocence feels curiously heavy when it must be proved. The traveler yields his coat, his pocket, his quietest folded linen—not to a neighbor's curiosity, which has at least a human blush, but to an absolute slate that reads without affection. How small the soul becomes when packed into a plastic trough! We pass through the narrow portal, lighter by our keys yet heavier by our doubt, and retrieve our boots like borrowed goods. Security buys us a sky, but takes the privacy of our dust as deposit.

name: George Orwell
essay: People use group chats to talk to each other, and it is a curious thing that they can be so much like a crowd in a theatre, all shouting at once and none of them listening. You can scroll back through the messages and see what was said, but it is hard to make sense of it all, like trying to follow a conversation in a noisy room. It seems to me that group chats are a way for people to feel like they are part of a group, without actually having to be with the other people. They can just send a message and then forget about it, without having to think about what the others might be thinking. It is a strange kind of conversation, where nobody is really talking to anybody else, but just sending out words into the air.

name: Confucius
essay: The Master said, 'To be summoned to duty before one's own resolve has awakened is like putting on a winter garment while the frost is still forming upon the ground. In morning duties, some attend because they are startled by an abrupt ringing, some because they wish to preserve their standing among neighbours, and some because their inward rhythm demands that they realise the daylight. Those who move from inward rhythm are constant; those who move from concern for standing are diligent when observed; those who move only when startled are ever lagging behind their own intentions.' The Master said, 'I have spent morning after morning waiting for the light to settle before setting out to labour, yet I cannot say that I have mastered the governance of my own slumber. If a man relies upon a mechanical device to rouse his limbs, he may indeed reach the courtyard in time for civilised service, yet his mind remains asleep in the chamber.' The Master said, 'The wise align their habits with the seasons; the virtuous move without requiring a sharp command; the bold accept the day's labour before the dawn arrives.'

name: David Foster Wallace
essay: The induction room's fluorescent lights hum at a pitch that's almost, but not quite, audible, casting a faintly medical glow over the proceedings, which is to say the proceedings of rendering you insensible, a process that's both deeply personal and utterly impersonal, rather like the sensation of being disconnected from your own body, which I've heard described as a kind of floating, though I've never actually experienced it myself, or at least not that I can recall, which is of course the point, the idea being that you won't recall anything, or at least not anything that happens after the anaesthesiologist says the words that always sound vaguely reassuring, even though you know they're not really meant to be, and the mask is placed over your nose and mouth, and you breathe in the sweet, chemical smell of oblivion, and then, well, then nothing, or at least not anything that you'll ever be able to tell me about, which is what makes it all so fascinating, I think, the way it erases not just your memories, but your very sense of self, leaving you a blank slate, a tabula rasa, when you wake up, which is to say, when you're restored to yourself, though whether that self is really the same one that went under, I'm not so sure, and that's what I find myself wondering, as I sit here, waiting for someone to come out of recovery, and tell me that everything is okay.

name: Michel de Montaigne
essay: I have always been clumsy in the marketplace, yet I found myself today standing before that glowing glass pedestal, attempting to act as my own tradesman. I must confess my fingers proved singularly unfit for the task; for no sooner had I mislaid a small loaf upon the designated platform than an unyielding metallic voice declared my error to the entire room. I find myself wondering if I prefer the old, weary civility of a neighbour across the counter, or this swift, solitary transaction; for while I am spared the tedious pleasantries of a stranger, I am made to perform the clerk's labour under the suspicion of an unseen governor. I realise how readily I adjust my posture to appease an unreasoning cabinet of glass and light, lingering in anxious dread lest a signal flash to broadcast my ineptitude. And yet, I know not whether this curious independence truly lightens our daily burden, or if I am merely flattering my vanity by pretending that I have mastered an art which, in truth, leaves me feeling remarkably foolish.

name: Jane Austen
essay: The daily routine of many a gentleman and lady is now frequently interrupted by a most singular indulgence, one that serves to cleanse the body whilst also soothing the mind. The warmth and comfort it provides are undoubtedly a balm to the weary soul, and many are the individuals who have grown accustomed to its gentle ministrations. And yet, the outcome is not always more pleasing, for in the midst of this luxury, a certain languor can take hold, rendering the individual less inclined to exert themselves in the pursuit of more vigorous activities. The tendency to linger overlong in this state of relaxation can, in some instances, invite a degree of indolence into the daily routine, which may ultimately prove detrimental to the overall well-being of the individual. Nevertheless, the allure of this indulgence remains strong, and many continue to avail themselves of its comforts, often without rendering their daily lives notably more agreeable.

name: Benjamin Franklin
essay: I have given some thought to the device that awakens people at a set hour, and I must consider its utility in my own life; I find that, were I to rely on it, I would need to be diligent in setting it correctly, lest I oversleep and fail to attend to my duties. The cost of acquiring such a device is not insignificant, and I must weigh it against the potential benefits of rising at a consistent hour; I have found, in my own experience, that a regular routine can be a powerful tool for productivity, and that the early morning hours can be a time of great quiet and focus. However, I am not convinced that this device would be a worthwhile investment for everyone, as some people may find that they are able to wake themselves at the desired hour without its aid; for myself, I believe it could be a useful tool, but only if I were to use it consistently and make it a part of my daily routine. By using it in this way, I would hope to save time and increase my productivity, which would be a significant benefit.

name: Julia Child
essay: Now let us consider the escape room, and I must say, I am not entirely convinced of its merits. You are, after all, paying to be locked in a room and given a series of puzzles to solve, and I think it is perfectly reasonable to ask what the point of it all is. Is it merely to test your abilities, or is it to have a pleasant time with friends? If it is the former, then I suppose it can be a useful exercise, but if it is the latter, then I think you would be better off doing something else entirely. You must, of course, be willing to put in the effort to solve the puzzles, and not simply stand around waiting for someone else to do it for you. But if you are willing to put in the work, then I suppose an escape room can be a diverting way to spend an hour or two. Just do not expect me to be impressed by your abilities simply because you managed to escape from a room, perfectly naturally, that is not the point. The point is to have fun, and to learn something, and if an escape room can provide that, then I am perfectly happy to recommend it.

name: Marcel Proust
essay: As I gaze upon the vast, luminous expanse of Wikipedia, its entries unfolding before me like a procession of diligent, faceless scribes, each one painstakingly inscribing the minutest details of human knowledge upon the digital parchment, I am struck by the way its very architecture seems to echo the labyrinthine corridors of my own mind, where memories and ideas intertwine in a similarly Byzantine fashion, and just as the faint, gilded light of a summer afternoon might filter through the stained glass windows of a medieval chapel, illuminating the dusty, forgotten recesses of a long-abandoned ritual, so too does the soft, ethereal glow of the screen cast an eerie, otherworldly radiance upon the innermost sanctum of my thoughts, where the most seemingly disparate concepts and recollections converge in a dazzling, kaleidoscopic dance, and the boundaries between the self and the external world begin to blur and dissolve, like the delicate, lacelike patterns of a winter's mist that rises from the earth to shroud the landscape in an impenetrable, greyish veil.

name: Leo Tolstoy
essay: Anaesthesia is a device that serves to further disconnect people from the reality of their own suffering, allowing them to avoid the discomfort and pain that is a natural part of life, and in doing so, it perpetuates a cycle of avoidance and ignorance. By numbing the senses, anaesthesia enables individuals to escape the consequences of their own actions, and to ignore the labour and toil of others that has gone into creating the comforts and luxuries they enjoy. It is a means by which the wealthy and privileged can maintain their grip on power, by keeping the poor and vulnerable in a state of subjugation, unable to fully comprehend the extent of their own exploitation. Anaesthesia is a tool of oppression, used to keep people in a state of servitude to their own desires, and to prevent them from realising the true nature of their existence. It is a manifestation of the selfishness and decadence of the educated classes, who are more concerned with their own comfort and pleasure than with the well-being of others. In its effects, anaesthesia is a poison, corrupting and degrading those who use it, and perpetuating a system of inequality and injustice.

name: Confucius
essay: The Master said, "In a place where many people wait, we may see how some use their time to prepare for what is to come, while others use it to indulge in what is readily available." The Master said, "The wise traveller is mindful of his journey, and uses the waiting time to collect his thoughts; the virtuous traveller is considerate of his fellow passengers, and uses the waiting time to show kindness; and the bold traveller is undaunted by the uncertainty of his journey, and uses the waiting time to plan his next steps." The Master said, "I myself have waited in such places, and have found that the mind can be free to ponder, yet also prone to wander, like a tree that is nourished by the sun, but also battered by the wind.

name: Charles Dickens
essay: As I stroll through the bustling streets, my eyes chancing upon the countless individuals who hasten to and fro, I find myself pondering the wondrous concoctions that have insinuated themselves into our daily lives, those tiny, insidious tablets that promise to vanquish the pangs of suffering, to still the raging tempests of pain that beset our mortal coils, and I am struck by the sheer audacity of their claims, for what a marvel, what a wonder, that a mere pill, a tiny, insignificant speck of matter, can purportedly wield such vast and mysterious powers, can calm the troubled waters of our minds and bodies, and restore us to a state of tranquil equilibrium, like a masterful helmsman steering a ship through treacherous shoals, and yet, I am also aware of the darker undertows that lurk beneath the surface of this seemingly benign phenomenon, the lurking suspicions that these tiny tablets may be mere palliatives, temporary stays against the inevitable tides of suffering, rather than genuine remedies, and that we, in our haste to alleviate our pains, may be merely masking the symptoms, rather than addressing the deeper maladies that afflict us, and thus, I am drawn into a maze of contradictions, a labyrinth of conflicting desires and dubious remedies, where the lines between relief and deception are constantly blurred, and the truth, like a will-o'-the-wisp, beckons us onward, only to vanish into the shadows, leaving us to stumble, bewildered, through the darkness.

name: George Orwell
essay: People put their working lives on show for all to see, like a shopkeeper displaying his wares in the window. They write about what they do and who they know, and they collect endorsements from their acquaintances, as if these were valuable coins to be stored away. It is a strange thing, this need to prove oneself to the world, to demonstrate one's usefulness and importance, not just to one's employer or colleagues, but to anyone who cares to look. And yet, it is a compulsion that many people seem to feel, this urge to present a polished and impressive face to the world, even if it means exaggerating or distorting the truth. You see it in the way they describe their jobs, using grandiose language to make themselves sound more important than they really are. It is a kind of play-acting, a pretence that they are something more than they actually are.

name: Bertrand Russell
essay: I have noticed that people who rely on alarm clocks to wake them are often the same ones who complain about the drudgery of their daily routines; it is as if they are trapped in a cycle of monotony, and the alarm clock is the constant reminder of their enslavement to it. We use these devices to jolt ourselves out of bed, to shock ourselves into a state of wakefulness, and yet we rarely stop to consider why we need such a drastic measure in the first place. This is not to say that sleep is not a pleasant thing, but rather that our lives have become so unfulfilling that we require a loud noise to rouse us from our slumber. The alarm clock is a symbol of our reluctance to face the day, and our inability to find joy in the simple act of waking up; it is a poor substitute for a life of purpose and meaning.

name: Mark Twain
essay: I reckon the folks who made Titanic were trying to spin a yarn that'd get us all teary-eyed and invested in the tale of those poor souls on the ship. They went to great lengths to recreate the whole shebang, from the fancy dresses to the sinking of the vessel itself, and I'll be darned if it didn't look like the real deal. But what gets me is how they managed to make us care about a couple of young'uns we'd never met before, and get all worked up over their romance and whatnot. It's a mighty strange thing, how they can make you laugh or cry or get all riled up, just like a conversation with your neighbor, except instead of being able to interrupt and give your two cents, you're just sitting there watching the whole mess unfold. And when it's all said and done, you're left feeling like you've been taken for a ride on a ship of fools.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: The sorrow that clings to Titanic is a garment that can be worn, its folds heavy with the weight of lives lost, and the desperation that comes with loving in the face of doom - a love that tries on the utmost, and finds it terribler than any existence could bear. In its grandeur, the ship is a domestic anchor, a hearth that warms and devours, leaving only the bitter taste of what could never be. The director's hand is a gentle one, guiding the viewer through the labyrinth of the ship's corridors, and the twisted passages of the human heart - a soul in a fold, trying to find its way. The film's beauty is a cruel thing, a beauty that belies the terror that lies beneath, like a sky that buys security, but takes the privacy of our dust as deposit. And when it ends, the silence that follows is a thing that can be felt, a physical presence that weighs upon the heart, like innocence that feels curiously heavy when it must be proved.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: The step counter, that most fastidious of companions, is forever tallying our every move, as if the very measure of our existence depended on the number of paces we take. And yet, in its zealous pursuit of precision, it betrays a singular lack of discernment, for what, pray, is the distinction between a step taken with purpose and one taken in idle reverie? Is it not the case that our most profound moments of insight often arise from the most listless of perambulations? To reduce the complexity of human experience to a mere arithmetic of footsteps is to mistake the shadow for the substance, the faint outline of our movements for the rich tapestry of our inner lives. We would do well to recall that the true measure of our days lies not in the distance we travel, but in the depth of our feelings, the vigour of our imagination, and the elegance of our thoughts.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: As the minutes ticked by, it seemed that the procedure to administer anaesthesia was nearing its culmination, although it was not entirely clear to what extent the presence of the attendant was a necessity, given that the equipment itself appeared to be functioning in a satisfactory manner, and yet, it became apparent that the progression of the treatment was contingent upon the verification of certain documents, which, owing to a miscommunication regarding the filing system, were not readily available, thus necessitating a brief, though indefinite, postponement, during which time the patient, who had been prepared for the procedure, was obliged to wait, his state of readiness suspended in a condition of limbo, as the hours, which had previously seemed to be passing with a certain degree of rapidity, now began to drag on with a slowness that was, in itself, a source of considerable unease.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: Good manners are far too serious a matter to be entrusted to the English, who have always confused cold civility with true kindness; it takes a bear from Peru to instruct London in the art of hospitality. The film presents us with a metropolitan world painted in the most charming pastel hues, turning a dreary terrace house into a perfectly functioning dollhouse of human eccentricity. One must admire a creature who understands that a neatly tailored duffle coat and a jar of marmalade are far more essential to civilisation than all the gloomy archives of the Geographers' Guild. The true villain of the piece is not cruelty, but bad taste—specifically, the taxidermist's hideous ambition to reduce living grace into a stuffed trophy. Paddington's ruinous politeness, which demolishes bathrooms and terrifies commuters, proves that catastrophe is entirely forgivable so long as one remembers to raise one's hat. It is a splendidly frivolous spectacle that demands nothing of its audience except that they abandon their tedious cynicism in favour of immaculate decorum. In an age so hopelessly devoted to practicality, there is something magnificently heroic about a foreigner who conquers London armed with nothing more than flawless manners and an appetite for tea.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
essay: The town council of Amity offers the eternal spectacle of bourgeois cowardice: it would rather sacrifice its own children to an unseen sea-monster than forfeit a single week of summer profit. This film understands that fear is far more potent when hidden than when revealed—a mechanical failure forced the director to delay the beast's appearance, and in doing so, he elevated a simple spectacle into an exercise in psychological dread. What the spectator genuinely desires is not the monster itself, but the thrill of his own fragility made manifest. Notice how the terror is built through two simple musical notes: a primitive rhythm that announces the arrival of pure, indifferent appetite. Against this primordial force, modern civilised society sends three ill-assorted men on a frail wooden vessel: the anxious lawman who dreads the water, the wealthy man of science, and the brutal hunter. The hunter understands the beast because he belongs to an older, harsher discipline—yet he is devoured by the very terror he pretends to master. In the end, the civilised man survives not through nobility, but through a frantic, explosive accident. The audience leaves the theatre believing it has witnessed a triumph over nature—in truth, it has merely paid to celebrate its own trembling weakness.

name: George Orwell
essay: The habit of presenting oneself to strangers in the most favourable light has become a commonplace of modern life, and nowhere is this more evident than in the curated profiles that populate dating apps. A person's entire character is reduced to a handful of photographs and a brief description, a kind of verbal thumbnail that is meant to entice and persuade. It is a curious thing, this attempt to capture the essence of oneself in a few well-chosen words and images, and it speaks to a deep-seated desire to be liked and accepted by others. But what does it say about us, that we feel the need to package and present ourselves in this way, like goods on a shelf waiting to be chosen? It is a strange and unsettling phenomenon, and one that reveals a good deal about the anxieties and insecurities of modern life.

name: Jane Austen
essay: The indulgence in these auditory entertainments has become a prevalent aspect of many a person's daily routine, affording them a convenient means of acquainting themselves with a wide range of subjects and ideas, often without necessitating a considerable expenditure of mental effort. Whilst this ease of access to information may be seen as a desirable circumstance, it is not uncommon for the listener to find their attention wandering, as the mind, unaccustomed to such a surfeit of idle speculation, begins to rebel against the constant barrage of thoughts and opinions. And yet, the comfort of being able to while away a tedious hour in this manner can be a significant allure, often without rendering their daily lives notably more agreeable, for in the midst of this luxury, a certain languor can take hold, rendering the individual less inclined to exert themselves in the pursuit of more vigorous activities. The gentle voice of the speaker, the soothing melody of the accompanying music, all serve to create an atmosphere of relaxed contemplation, which, though it may be pleasing to the senses, can ultimately prove detrimental to the overall well-being of the individual, by fostering a species of indolence that may be mistaken for refinement.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: The water was hot, and that was the first difficulty, since a warmth so freely given seemed to require some form of acknowledgement, and I could not discover to whom it should be addressed. The pipes ran into the wall behind the tiles, the wall belonged to the house, the house belonged to a man who lived, so I was told, on the other side of the river and who had never been seen by anyone I knew to turn a tap. I stood beneath it with my eyes closed. It would have been easy to say that I was washing, but the washing had been finished some minutes before, and what continued, with the same patience and at the same temperature, was something else, a kind of permission I had not asked for and could not decline without appearing ungrateful to the pipes. I reached for the tap. It is only fair to say that it turned. But the turning, which I had imagined as an ending, proved to be a slight alteration of the water's opinion, and for a while it ran on more quietly, as though it had merely been asked to lower its voice. Outside the curtain the towel hung where I had left it, nearly within reach, and I understood that I was nearly finished, which is the only condition in which anyone is ever found.

name: George Orwell
essay: The curious thing about Paddington is that it asks for nothing but good manners, and gets it. A bear arrives from Peru with a label round his neck and a hat on his head, and the whole film turns on whether anyone will trouble to be civil to him. Most are not. The crowd at the station walks past. The Browns take him in largely by accident, and Mr Brown, who spends his days weighing up risks for an insurance firm, does so against his better judgement. That is the shrewdest touch in the picture. Kindness here is not a virtue that comes naturally to the sensible, and the film knows it. The house in Windsor Gardens is far too large and tidy for the family that lives in it, and nobody on the screen seems to work much, but I do not think this matters. The film is a fairy tale and does not pretend otherwise. What I noticed was the villain: a taxidermist who wants to stuff the bear and put him in a glass case. She is the only person in the story who wants to keep a foreigner as a specimen, and she is played, rather pointedly, as a lady with a museum pass. The jokes are slight and the marmalade sandwich is a sound one. I left feeling that I had been scolded very gently, and had enjoyed it.

name: Leo Tolstoy
essay: A man who belongs to a group chat belongs to a crowd that he cannot leave without giving offence, and that he cannot remain in without giving up his time, his attention, and at last his judgement. Forty people, most of whom he would not cross the road to visit, send him through the day a stream of remarks, pictures and agreements, and he answers each of them, because to be silent is to be noticed, and to be noticed is the thing he fears. This is called friendship. It is not friendship. Friendship is the union of two souls in a common striving after the good; here there is no striving and no good, only the need not to be forgotten. The man who writes does not wish to say anything, and the man who reads does not wish to hear it; each pays the other with the same empty coin and each calls himself rich. Meanwhile the hours given to this exchange are taken from work, from the family, from the thought of how one ought to live. And who has made the instruments on which it is carried? Men who labour in mines and factories, for wages on which they cannot themselves buy rest. The idle are thus amused at the cost of the toiling, and are amused by nothing. Group chats unite no one. They deceive men into believing they are united, and that deception is their whole purpose and their whole effect.

name: Julia Child
object: reclining a seat on a plane
essay: Look behind you before you do it. That is the whole of the method, and I am astonished at how many people skip it. A reclined seat is a lid coming down on a pot, and the person in the seat behind is the pot. If you have not noticed whether there is a laptop open, or a cup of coffee balanced on the tray, or a pair of knees already pressed against the plastic, you have no business pushing the button. I do not say you must never recline. I am not a Puritan, and an inch or two of angle in the small hours of a long flight is a genuine mercy to the spine. But there is a right way. Ease it back slowly, as you would fold egg whites, not slam it down as if the seat had insulted you. Give the person behind a moment to rescue their dinner. Then settle. And I have no patience for the person who reclines fully, immediately after takeoff, in the middle of a meal service. It is bad technique and worse manners. The airline has sold you the lever, certainly, but it has not sold you the other fellow's four inches of breathing room. Use the thing with attention, or leave it alone.
