name: Charles Dickens
essay: I met him on the Hungerford stairs at eleven at night, a respectable man of fifty with the collar of a deacon, and he was laughing. He was laughing alone, at nothing, at the river, at the lamp, with his mouth open and his head thrown back, as if the very fog had told him a joke. Two paces on I saw the cause: a small white wire dangled from each of his ears like the roots of some bloodless vegetable, and into that wire two gentlemen, whom he had never met and never would, were pouring an hour and forty minutes of their opinions upon cheese. I do not object to the opinions. I object to the hour and forty minutes. Here are two persons who, in my own day, must have been put to some honest trade, and who now are permitted to prattle without interruption, without correction, without so much as a cough from a bored relation, and to be conveyed in the pocket to every pillow in the kingdom! Nobody stops them. Nobody ever says, Gentlemen, enough. And the listener, poor captive, walks the whole length of London in their company, deaf to the cab, deaf to the beggar, deaf to the plain, unadvertised music of his own thoughts, which have been turned out of doors like a tenant in arrears.

name: George Orwell
essay: My grandmother's cure for toothache was a clove held against the gum and a good deal of patience. It did not work very well, and nobody pretended it did. The tooth went on aching until it was pulled, and in the meantime one learned what an ache was, how it rose at night and fell in the morning, and how far it could be borne. I do not say this was an education worth having. I say only that it was one. Now the ache is dealt with before it has properly begun. Two white tablets in a glass of water, and in twenty minutes the headache has gone, the back has stopped complaining, and the man at the next desk, who has also taken two, is typing as though nothing were the matter with either of them. Nobody can object to this. Pain is a bad thing, and anyone who tells you otherwise has generally got a comfortable chair. But it is worth noticing what the tablet does besides relieve. It makes pain a private failing, something to be cleared up quietly so that the work need not stop. The headache that might have said the room is too hot, the hours too long, the foreman too loud, is silenced before it can say anything. A great deal of complaint used to be carried by the body. We have found a cheap way of not listening to it.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: The man in the next lane was moving his lips. Not singing, not cursing, just mouthing along to something only he could hear, and when we stalled together at the light on Route 9 I saw the little glowing rectangle on his dashboard and the title scrolling across it, a novel I had once read in a motel in Tucson with a wet towel under the door and a very bad conscience. He was being read to. At sixty miles an hour. By a stranger with a trained voice and a union card. I have no quarrel with the story. My quarrel is with the voice, that smooth professional baritone doing the dialogue of a drunken sheriff as if he were reading the specials at a steakhouse. Prose has a pulse of its own, a bad, crooked, private one, and the narrator has stolen it and sold it back to you at a markup. You no longer hear the book. You hear a man's opinion of the book, delivered in your skull while your hands do something else. And that is the real swindle: the idea that attention can be split like a check. It cannot. Somebody always gets shorted, usually the road. He drove off, still mouthing. I let the light change twice.

name: Virginia Woolf
essay: There is a particular voice that lives in the machine at the end of the aisle, and it says, with the serenity of a governess who has never been contradicted, that there is an unexpected item in the bagging area. Nothing is there but a lemon. Yet we stand, the lemon and I, convicted, while a small light turns on above our heads like a flag run up over a fortress, and across the shop a girl in a green apron begins, without haste, to walk towards us. Let us consider what has been taken from the transaction, and what has been left. The cashier used to sit at her post for eight hours, and in eight hours a face grows into its place; she knew who bought the gin on Fridays, who counted out coppers, who lingered because the house at home was quiet. We were looked at, and being looked at is a small, steady tax upon the soul that we did not know we were glad to pay. Now nobody looks. We perform her labour, unpaid, under the eye of a glass lens, and are thanked by a recording. But the girl in green arrives, taps the screen, and sighs, and in that sigh, shared between two people who both despise the contrivance, something old and human flickers back into the shop.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: Thou wilt be asked to remove thy belt. Remove it. The belt was never thine in any way that matters. Thou wilt stand in a line. A line is only men waiting, and thou art one of them. Thou art no more the exception here than anywhere. The man who looks into thy bag does his work. He did not choose thee. He sees a thousand bags before noon. Give him no cause for contempt, and take none from him. Thou fearest delay. Examine the fear. The hour is not stolen from thee, since it was never promised. Thou hast only the present, and the present is here, between two plastic trays. They ask whether thou carriest anything sharp. Answer plainly. Thou carriest much that is sharp, and none of it is in the bag: the quick word, the sneer at the slow traveller, the claim that thou art owed haste. The machine looks through thy coat and finds nothing. Let it find nothing in thy temper either. They fear what a few men might do. The fear is not foolish, and not thine to mock. Thou also hast guarded a gate against a smaller enemy and called it prudence. Walk through when thou art called. Put on thy shoes. Hold thy tongue.

name: Douglas Adams
essay: The airport lounge works on a principle that would be familiar to anyone who has studied the medieval sale of indulgences: you pay a considerable sum so that you may wait in a better place for the thing you are already waiting for. The thing does not arrive any sooner. It is simply that, while it fails to arrive, you are permitted to sit in a chair that was chosen by someone who had once read about chairs. The lounge is defined chiefly by what it is not, and what it is not is the terminal, which stands a few feet away on the other side of a door that has been fitted with a very serious receptionist. Behind her, everything is the same as outside, only quieter and free, and it is the free that does the work. A person who would not dream of eating a lukewarm sandwich at eleven in the morning will eat three of them, standing up, because they have been included in the price. Nobody in the history of commerce has been so thoroughly persuaded by a sandwich. The real function of the place, I suspect, is to reassure the traveller that the delay is happening to someone of standing. The departures board says the same thing in the lounge as it does everywhere else, but it says it on a better screen, and this is felt, quite sincerely, to be a form of progress.

name: Confucius
essay: The Master said, 'When a man is asked to take off his belt and his shoes before strangers, and does so without complaint, I do not yet know whether he is patient or only tired.' The Master said, 'The officer who looks into my bag may be diligent, or fearful, or merely obedient. The diligent look at the traveller. The fearful look at the bag. The obedient look at the line behind him.' The Master said, 'I have stood a long while in such a line, and my thoughts were not good ones. I counted the faults of the man ahead of me, who had forgotten his coins, and I did not count my own, which were the same.' The Master said, 'A gate that is kept in order is a courtesy of a kind. It says that the road is shared, and that no one has the right to endanger another. But where the gate is kept with suspicion toward all, trust is spent faster than it is earned.' The Master said, 'When the officer says "Please" and means it, the line moves more easily than any machine could move it. When he says it as a rule, it does not.' The Master said, 'I would put up with the shoes. It is the manner of asking that I should wish to see mended, in the one who asks and in the one who answers.'

name: Nora Ephron
essay: The marmalade sandwich under the hat is the thing I keep thinking about. Not the sandwich itself, which is a joke, but the fact that he keeps it there for emergencies, the way my mother kept a twenty-dollar bill folded into the toe of a boot. Paddington is a bear who has been told that London will be kind, and the movie's whole nerve is that it lets him be wrong for about an hour and a half and then makes him right anyway. I went expecting to be charmed and to resent it. I was charmed. I resented nothing. Hugh Bonneville plays the father as a man who has calculated the risk of everything, including breakfast, and I recognized him at once; I have dated him. Nicole Kidman, in her ice-blond bob and her taxidermy kit, is the only villain I have ever wanted to see in a better coat. What the film wants from you is simple. It wants you to say hello to a stranger on the Tube escalator, and it knows you won't, and it forgives you in advance. That's the trick. It is so polite that you leave feeling vaguely accused, and also, I'm sorry to say, hungry. I bought a jar of Dundee marmalade on the way home. It's still in the cupboard. I'm saving it.

name: Marcel Proust
essay: What strikes me, when the face of one of these young women appears on the little lit pane of my telephone, recommending with a radiance of perfectly rehearsed spontaneity a serum, a hotel in the Maldives, a way of folding linen, is not that she is lying, for she is probably sincere, but that her sincerity has been so thoroughly lit from every side, like those portraits by fashionable painters in which the sitter's pearls are rendered with such care that we begin to suspect the sitter herself was added afterwards to give the pearls somewhere to hang, that we can no longer find the spot where the woman ends and the commission begins. I have known, in the salons of my youth, duchesses who made a fashion merely by arriving late in a particular shade of mauve, and their power seemed to me mysterious because it was never confessed; theirs was the authority of a name that had no need to ask. These others ask constantly, and are therefore loved with that peculiar tenderness we reserve for people who flatter us by needing us, so that the multitude, which believes it is following her, is really being counted by her, each admirer a small coin dropped into a purse whose weight she consults between sentences. And yet I cannot quite despise her, since I too once bought a cravat because a man I admired wore one, and wore it, I now suspect, because someone else had.

name: Bertrand Russell
essay: I have been told that a man may now listen to two strangers talk for three hours about a subject on which neither is an authority, and that millions do so willingly. My first impulse was to condemn this. My second was to remember how I have spent a good many evenings, and to hold my tongue. Talk is the oldest of our entertainments, and it was never meant to be edited. The dinner table, the club, the railway carriage supplied it free, and the quality was uneven. What has changed is that the dull remark, once confined to the room in which it was made, can now be preserved and distributed to the whole world. I do not think this has made us wiser; I think it has made us better supplied. Still, there is one real merit. The listener's hands are free, and a man who is washing dishes while hearing an argument about the Roman provinces is better occupied than a man who is washing dishes with nothing in his head but his grievances. Most people's private thoughts are not good company. The danger is that we shall mistake hearing a conversation for taking part in one. Agreeing with a voice in the kitchen costs nothing, and it is worth about that.

name: Henry David Thoreau
essay: I went to see the ogre because I was told he lived in a swamp, and I confess I was prepared to like any man who would. He has the sense to keep a mud-hole of his own, a onion for his supper, and a sign on his fence; he asks of the world only that it stay on the far side of the post. For perhaps ten minutes this is the best economy on the screen. Then the swamp is overrun by eviction notices and fairy-tale refugees, and he must trot off to win it back from a lord who is, I take it, five feet tall and owns a castle. The bargain is this: he is to fetch a princess in exchange for his own quiet. I have known farmers strike worse ones, and for less mud. What I cannot forgive is the manner. Every minute of the picture, perhaps ninety-odd of them, is paid for in jokes about other stories, so that the audience laughs only at what it has already been sold elsewhere. The wolf, the pig, the gingerbread man are brought in like borrowed tools and returned unsharpened. The donkey talks as fast as a clerk paid by the word. Yet when the ogre's breath fogs a window in the morning light, or a dragon's chain swings over a lake of real fire, I was caught entirely, and would have stayed the night. The moral, that the green man is as good as the pink, is sound, and cheap, and costs the makers nothing to say.

name: Julia Child
essay: A dinner party for twelve works because someone decides who sits where. Put the same twelve people in a room with no host, no table and no hour at which to go home, and you have a group chat. I cannot say I admire it. Consider what goes wrong. Everyone speaks at once, nobody waits for the sauce to finish, and a question about Saturday is answered on Tuesday by someone who has plainly not read the first forty messages. The cook in me is appalled. Conversation, like a good stock, wants proportion and a little patience, and here is a pot into which every guest throws whatever is in his pocket. And yet I will not be entirely sour about it. When a sister reports that the roast is out of the oven and the family may come, and nine people answer within a minute, that is a table of a sort. That is useful, and rather lovely. So here is my method. Keep the group small, as you would a sauce with few ingredients. Give it one purpose. Say plainly what you mean, once, and then stop. Mute it when you must, without apology, as you would close the kitchen door on a noisy dog. And for anything that matters, a birthday, a quarrel, a death, telephone, or better, go and sit down together.
